summaries.example: Imagine two adults who promise to care for each other. They may also share money, work, or care for children. One question is whether their promises should be whatever they choose, or whether marriage has important rules that come with the role. Another question is whether the law should treat different kinds of loving families fairly.
summaries.summary: The entry explains that marriage is more than one thing: it can be a legal status, a religious practice, and a way people organize family life. Across history and cultures, marriages have involved love, friendship, children, money, work, inheritance, and ties between families. Because marriage varies so much, some philosophers say it has no single essential shape. Others offer a preferred definition based on an ethical purpose, such as raising children or supporting committed love. A major debate compares the contractual view with the institutional view. The contractual view treats marriage duties mainly as promises that partners may arrange or change. The institutional view says marriage has a purpose that gives it duties even when partners would prefer different rules. Philosophers also debate divorce, sexual exclusivity, marriage law, same-sex marriage, and whether marriage should be replaced or reformed. Feminist and queer critiques examine how marriage has sometimes supported unequal gender roles, excluded people, or favored one kind of relationship. The central lesson is that deciding what marriage should be requires thinking about history, fairness, freedom, love, family care, and the role of government.
key_ideas: Marriage has not looked the same in every culture or time period. It can be a legal status, a religious ceremony, and a social practice.
Some philosophers think spouses should choose most marriage rules themselves, like people making a contract.
Other philosophers think marriage has a purpose, such as caring for children or protecting a loving partnership, and that this purpose creates duties.
Philosophers ask why governments recognize marriage and give married people special legal benefits.
Feminist and queer philosophers ask whether marriage has supported unfair gender or relationship rules, and whether it should be changed.
summaries.why_it_matters: Marriage can affect people’s homes, money, care responsibilities, family relationships, and legal protection. Thinking carefully about it helps us ask whether laws are fair and whether they protect people who may have less power. It also reminds us that a custom being old does not automatically make it just, and that changing a law can help some people while raising new questions for others.

important_terms.definition: A legally recognized relationship that can bring duties, protections, and benefits.
A promise or agreement between people or groups.
A set of social rules and roles that lasts over time, such as marriage or school.
Fair treatment and fair chances for people.
The idea that people should be free to make important choices for themselves.

questions_to_think_about: What should make a relationship important to the law?
Should people be able to choose all the promises made in a marriage?
Can marriage protect love, or can its rules sometimes make life harder?
How can laws protect people inside families when love or trust breaks down?

summaries.example: Suppose two adults enter a marriage but agree that either may end it whenever they wish, while also promising to share childcare and property fairly. A contractual theorist may ask what promises they actually made and whether either spouse released the other from them. An institutional theorist may ask whether marriage carries duties that cannot be removed by private agreement. A political philosopher then asks why the state should attach tax, inheritance, immigration, or caregiving benefits to marriage rather than to separate relationships or caregiving roles.
summaries.summary: The entry presents marriage as a contested legal, social, and sometimes religious institution. Its historical forms have included economic and political alliances, kinship arrangements, procreative unions, religious sacraments, contracts, and relationships of companionship. This variety supports the view that “marriage” may function as a family-resemblance concept rather than having one descriptive essence. Yet descriptive history cannot decide the normative question of what marriage should be: a proposed definition must be defended by ethical and political reasons. The main moral dispute in the entry is between contractual and institutional accounts. Contractual accounts treat marital obligations as promises, making questions of consent, renegotiation, release, adultery, divorce, and the possibility of promising love central. Institutional accounts hold that the role’s purpose fixes obligations. New natural law theories identify procreation and marital friendship as the relevant goods; other institutional theories see marriage as a structure that supports committed love, though they disagree about whether exclusivity is necessary. Political philosophy asks why the state should recognize marriage, restrict entry or exit, distribute benefits through it, and protect property or caregiving interests. Arguments for same-sex marriage emphasize equal treatment, equal citizenship, and the value of legal recognition; objections appeal to procreation, sexual difference, or possible effects on family life. Feminist and queer critiques challenge marriage’s historical gender hierarchy and its tendency to privilege heterosexual, exclusive, couple-centered relationships. key_ideas: Historical and cultural variation makes it difficult to infer a single descriptive essence of marriage. A past legal definition also cannot by itself settle what marriage ought to be.

The contractual view grounds marital obligations in promises and voluntary undertaking. It raises questions about releasing one another from exclusivity or permanence, and about whether one can promise to love.
Institutional theories argue that marriage’s purpose supplies obligations. Major versions emphasize a procreative union or the protection of a valuable love relationship.
Marriage is a legally unusual contract: its terms are often supplied by law, its benefits affect third parties, and its rules can protect people when affection or bargaining power fails.

Arguments for recognizing same-sex marriage commonly appeal to equality, equal citizenship, and the recognition of intimate relationships. Arguments against it often appeal to a different-sex or procreative definition, though those arguments face challenges about infertile or childless marriages.

Feminist and queer critiques connect marriage to gender inequality, care work, abuse, racial exclusion, class inequality, and pressure to fit one relationship model. Reform proposals range from changing marriage law to replacing marriage with other legal arrangements.
summaries.why_it_matters: Marriage law distributes recognition, resources, rights, and risks. It can protect intimate partners and dependent caregivers, but it can also preserve unequal divisions of labor, make economic dependence harder to escape, or exclude relationships that do not fit dominant norms. Philosophical analysis helps separate empirical claims from moral claims: for example, whether marriage benefits children is partly an empirical question, while whether the state may promote marriage is a question about justice, liberty, and neutrality.

important_terms.definition: The view that marital duties are primarily voluntary promises whose content spouses may negotiate or, in some cases, waive.
The view that marriage has a purpose that determines duties spouses cannot simply redesign by agreement.
A concept whose examples share overlapping similarities rather than one feature common to every case.
The idea that special duties arise from voluntary acts such as promises or agreements.
A political view that the state should avoid basing law on disputed ideas about the best way to live.
The belief that laws and institutions should not unfairly favor or burden people because of group membership or relationship type.
A theory that identifies procreation and marital friendship as central human goods and as the basis of marriage.
The expectation that heterosexuality and gender difference are the standard forms of intimate life.

questions_to_think_about: If marriage is voluntary, which obligations may spouses negotiate, and which—if any—should remain fixed?
Can the state justify special marriage benefits without endorsing a controversial ideal of love, sex, or family life?
Does equal treatment require the same legal status for same-sex and different-sex couples, or can a different distinction be morally relevant?
Would separating parenting, caregiving, and relationship recognition produce fairer laws?
Can marriage be reformed to reduce inequality, or do its basic social meanings make abolition more attractive?

summaries.example: Imagine a school club whose members agree to help one another. One student says the members should choose every rule. Another says the club has a purpose—helping students learn—and some rules follow from that purpose. Philosophers use a similar contrast when discussing marriage. Is it mainly a set of promises made by partners, or is it an institution with duties connected to love, family care, or children? The answer can affect views about divorce and other relationships.
summaries.summary: The entry examines marriage as a subject of moral and political philosophy. Marriage can mean a civil status, a religious rite, or a social practice, and its forms differ widely across time and place. Historically, it has often organized property, inheritance, labor, and kinship; the modern emphasis on romantic love is not timeless. This variety leads some philosophers to resist searching for one essential definition. Others argue that marriage should be defined normatively, using a view about what it is for. Two broad approaches organize the moral debate. On the contractual approach, marriage creates special obligations through promises. Partners may therefore have some power to set terms or release one another, although parental duties or other serious duties may remain. This view must explain why marriage is more than any private agreement. On the institutional approach, the purpose of marriage determines obligations that partners cannot simply rewrite. One major version treats marriage as a procreative union connected with raising children and marital friendship. Another treats it as a framework that protects committed love, while philosophers disagree about whether love requires sexual exclusivity. Political arguments ask whether marriage should receive state recognition and benefits, whether laws should make divorce easier or harder, and how to protect people from economic inequality or abuse. Same-sex marriage debates commonly appeal to equal treatment and equal citizenship. Critics may argue that marriage is essentially different-sex or procreative, but the entry considers challenges involving infertile couples, childless couples, and changing legal meanings. key_ideas: Marriage has changed across history and cultures. It has sometimes focused more on property, family alliances, work, or inheritance than on romantic love.
Some philosophers think marriage is a family-resemblance idea: different marriages can share similarities without all having one defining feature.
The contractual view says marital duties are largely promises. This can support personal freedom, but it may not explain why marriage is a special institution.
The institutional view says marriage has a purpose that creates duties. Some versions focus on having and raising children; others focus on protecting committed love.
Marriage is not an ordinary private contract because law connects it with taxes, inheritance, immigration, caregiving, and divorce.
Debates about same-sex marriage involve equality and recognition, but also questions about the purpose of marriage and whether old definitions should control new legal decisions.
summaries.why_it_matters: Marriage rules can shape who receives legal protection, who performs unpaid care, how property is shared, and whose relationships are treated as fully respectable. Studying the issue shows why familiar institutions need reasons, not just tradition. It also shows that a fair policy must consider both freedom to form relationships and protection against unequal power within them.

important_terms.definition: A legally recognized relationship with rules, responsibilities, and possible benefits.
An agreement in which people make promises or set terms for their relationship.
A lasting social arrangement with roles and rules, such as a family, school, or government.
The idea that marriage should be understood through its purpose rather than only through the promises partners make.
The idea that partners should have major control over the duties and rules of their marriage.
Fairness in how people are treated and in the chances they receive.
The belief that laws should not favor one disputed idea about a good life over others.

questions_to_think_about: Should a marriage be allowed to have any rules that both partners choose?
Why might a government give marriage special legal benefits?
Does a relationship need children or the possibility of children to count as a marriage?
Could a law be equal in money and benefits but still unequal in social respect?
What might be gained or lost by replacing marriage with several different legal statuses?
